claims.text: The proposed physics-informed machine-learning framework explicitly uses oxygen content and defect-induced local lattice distortion features.
Including oxygen content and defect-induced distortions will significantly improve conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr over conventional perfect-crystal analytical models.
Electrical transport from 0–200 K in the specified alloy is dominated by ionized-impurity scattering.
Electrical transport from 300–1200 K in the specified alloy is dominated by phonon scattering.
Bulk HfNbTaTiZr made by standard synthesis routes contains point defects and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen in practice.
The regression model will incorporate temperature-dependent scattering terms, defect statistics, and oxygen concentration as inputs.
The test sample must contain approximately 1 wt.% oxygen and be evaluated within 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Oxygen produces point defects and associated local lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen-related point defects and local lattice distortions modulate electron-scattering mechanisms.
Established scattering theories distinguish impurity and phonon contributions to carrier mobility.
Combining physical scattering models with data-driven calibration can provide learning capability together with physical interpretability and generalization.
Calibration against experimental conductivity data will correct oxygen and defect effects neglected by analytical approaches.
Accounting jointly for impurity and phonon scattering will capture temperature-dependent conductivity more faithfully.
The model will have a statistically significantly lower conductivity mean absolute error than defect-free analytical models.
The analytical baseline assumes an ideal perfect crystal and omits defect scattering and oxygen impurities.
The hypothesis is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen and to 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Spectroscopic or diffraction-based methods can accurately determine oxygen content and defect density.

The hypothesis is falsified if held-out conductivity predictions fail to show a statistically significant improvement, exemplified as more than a 10% MAE reduction, over the analytical baseline in both temperature regimes.
